title: The Contaminated Control

scenario.situation: A referral-incentive experiment ran for four weeks. Treatment users received a bonus for inviting friends. Post-test, control users also showed a meaningful activity bump — nearly half the lift seen in treatment — and the team is questioning whether the test is valid at all.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The PM believes the experiment is broken or inconclusive and wants to scrap the results and rerun.
scenario.question: Is the test really broken, or is something explainable happening?

decisions.prompt: The PM wants to declare the test invalid and rerun it. How do you frame your investigation before agreeing?

options.label: Audit the randomization pipeline
options.detail: Check whether users were accidentally assigned to the wrong group due to a bug.
options.consequence: The randomization code checks out — users were correctly assigned. You've ruled out a bug, but you still have no explanation for the control lift. The PM is no more convinced the test is salvageable.
options.divergenceCost: Assumed a technical failure and spent effort ruling out the wrong cause.

options.label: Segment by social connection to treatment users
options.detail: Ask: did control users who are direct friends of treatment users behave differently from control users with no treatment connections?
options.consequence: Splitting control users by whether they were invited or connected to a treatment user reveals that the lift is concentrated among socially adjacent controls. The test isn't broken — treatment leaked across the network boundary.

options.label: Extend the test duration and rerun
options.detail: Accept the PM's framing and relaunch the experiment with a longer window.
options.consequence: A rerun with the same individual-level randomization scheme produces the same spillover pattern. You've lost four more weeks and still have no clean read.
options.divergenceCost: Accepted the stakeholder's conclusion without diagnosing the root cause first.

options.label: Compare control-group time series to a pre-experiment baseline
options.detail: Check if control activity was already trending up before the experiment launched.
options.consequence: The pre-experiment trend is flat for control users, so a secular trend isn't the culprit. You've eliminated one alternative but still can't explain where the control lift came from.
options.divergenceCost: Investigated a plausible but ultimately unrelated alternative explanation, making no progress on the real driver.

decisions.prompt: You split the control group by social proximity to treatment users. Which metric best confirms whether interference is the driver?

artifact.title: Average weekly activity change — all control users vs. treatment users
artifact.caption: Raw average lift. Control shows nearly half the treatment lift — suspicious, but pooling all control users hides what matters.

options.label: Raw average activity lift: treatment vs. all control users
options.detail: Use the aggregate averages already in the experiment dashboard.
options.consequence: The aggregate view confirms control lifted, but it can't tell you why. You still can't distinguish a real spillover from a seasonal effect or a platform-wide nudge. The PM's 'inconclusive' verdict stands.
options.divergenceCost: Used an aggregate metric that pools clean and contaminated controls, masking the interference signal.

options.label: Activity lift by control-user exposure tier (connected vs. unconnected to treatment)
options.detail: Compute the lift separately for (1) control users who received an invite from a treatment user and (2) control users with zero treatment connections.
options.consequence: The segmented view is unambiguous: unexposed control users show near-zero lift, while control users connected to a treatment user show a lift nearly matching the treatment group itself. The interference pathway is visible and measurable.

artifact.title: Activity lift by group and exposure tier
artifact.caption: Unexposed controls barely moved. The 'control lift' was entirely driven by users who crossed the network boundary — classic interference.

decisions.prompt: Connected control users show nearly the same lift as treatment users, while unconnected controls show almost none. What do you tell the PM?

options.label: "The incentive works — contaminated controls prove it spreads organically. Ship the feature."
options.detail: Use the spillover itself as evidence of a positive network effect and recommend launch.
options.consequence: You've made a causal leap: the measured treatment effect is almost certainly underestimated (because some 'control' users already got the benefit), and the true incremental lift is unknown. Shipping based on a diluted effect size could mean over- or under-investing in the incentive.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a clean causal estimate from a contaminated experiment.

options.label: "The test isn't broken — it has network interference. The true effect is underestimated; rerun with cluster randomization to get a clean read before deciding on rollout."
options.detail: Name the interference mechanism, explain the implication for the effect size, and prescribe cluster-level randomization.
options.consequence: The PM now understands why control lifted, why the current effect estimate is a lower bound, and what a valid rerun looks like. You've saved the learning from being discarded and given a clear, actionable path to a trustworthy answer.

insight: The control group lifted because treatment users invited their friends who happened to be in the control group — a textbook violation of the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA). The experiment wasn't broken; it was randomized at the wrong level. The fix is cluster randomization (e.g., by friend group or geographic community) so that treatment and control users don't share a social boundary. The lesson: on social or referral products, individual-level A/B tests almost always underestimate true effects because the network transmits the treatment.
